messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to fit a VC model using:

    formula<-Y ~ 1 + f(iid, model="iid",
                     hyper=list(theta=list(prior="loggamma", param=c(1E-03,1E-03))))

    model<-inla(formula,
                   family="gaussian",
                   data=mydata,
                   quantiles=c(0.025,0.25,0.5,0.75,0.975))

and I would like to specify the prior, not only for the hyper parameter of the random effects, i.e. "iid" term, but also for the residual variance of the
"gaussian" model. My question is if it is possible, and what is the default prior used for the residual variance by INLA??

Thanks,

--Ehsan

>                      hyper=list(theta=list(prior="loggamma",
> param=c(1E-03,1E-03))))
>

>                    family="gaussian",
>                    data=mydata,
>                    quantiles=c(0.025,0.25,0.5,0.75,0.975))
>
> and I would like to specify the prior, not only for the hyper
> parameter of the random effects, i.e. "iid" term, but also for the
> residual variance of the
> "gaussian" model. My question is if it is possible, and what is the
> default prior used for the residual variance by INLA??

Hi, you can define the prior for the precision in the Gaussian responce
in the same way (see inla.doc("gaussian")), using the control.family
variable,

inla(...,

control.family = list(hyper = list(prec = list(
				prior = "loggamma",
				param = c(1, 0.0001))))

'prec', 'precision', 'theta' are all various names for the same
precision parameter (see the inla.doc(...)).

the Gamma(eps,eps) prior is know to be very bad, and its discussed for
example here

@Article{art460,
  author =       {Y. Fong and H. Rue and J. Wakefield},
  title =        {Bayesian inference for Generalized Linear Mixed
                  Models},
  journal =      {Biostatistics},
  year =         2010,
  volume =       11,
  number =       3,
  pages =        {397--412}
}

There is also a new concept of 'penalized complexity priors' which
suggest an exponential prior on the stdev scale. see http://arxiv.org/a
bs/1403.4630 and read v3 which is the better one.   this prior is avail
as  prior = "pc.prec", param = c(U, alpha), see inla.doc("pc.prec")

H

b) Is anyone doing so?

Many thanks!
Jacob Davies

messages.body_plain:
I have a question about the accuracy of R-INLA case study code, specifically Blangiardo et a. 2012 code that uses London Suicides data.

Here  <http://www.r-inla.org/examples/volume-1/code-for-bym-example>it says that “[if you] use the combined model BYM, which contains both the “iid” and the “besag” model...This makes it possible to get the marginals of “iid” + “besag” which otherwise is only possible using linear combinations.

This is what I would like to do – that is, get the marginals of iid+besag, instead of the marginal of iid only or besag only.

The Blangiardo et al. 2012 code <http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/case-studies/Blangiardo-et-al-2012/Code/LondonSuicides.R> (London Suicides) says the following:

#We calculate zeta=exp(csi) where csi=upsilon + nu

m <- mod$marginals.random$ID[1:Nareas]  ###note that Nareas=32, the number of spatial units
zeta <- lapply(m,function(x) inla.emarginal(exp,x))

But, while there are only 32 regions (Nareas=32), the output from Blangiardo's model actually has 64 random effects (32 iid, 32 besag). This can be seen by:
> dim(mod$summary.random$ID)
[1]64 8

Also, this:
> length(mod$marginals.random$ID)
64

So doesn't random.marginals[1:32] correspond to marginal for the iid random effects, and random.marginals[33:64] correspond to the besag random effects??

Then how is Blangiardo calculating  “zeta=exp(csi) where csi=upsilon +nu” when they only extract the marginals for the first 32 random effects (Nareas=32)????

What about marginals for the besag/spatial random effects, those which seem to be found in mod$marginals.random$ID[33:64]?? (I checked, and there are numbers there)

Thank you in advance for any help. It is greatly appreciated.

Just to add more information, in the case it helps for further discussion.

The mixed model is the same for all approaches:

y = Xb + Za + e

where,

y = observations (phenotypes)
X = matrix accounting fixed effects
b = vector of fixed effects for each observation
Z = matrix addressing jth marker information within the ith animal
a = marker effects
e = residual term (noise)

As I said, each approach considers different prior distribution for a.

So, in...

GBLUP - ai ~ N(0, sigma[a]^2)

Bayes A - ai ~ t(0, v, sigma[a]^2)
also, for Meuwissen,

ai ~N(0, sigma[ai]^2) quiSqrd[v]^-2 sigma[a]^-2

Bayes B - ai ~ pi(0) + (1-pi)t(0,v, sigma[a]^2)
(a fraction "pi" of markers has zero effect and another (1-pi) fraction has t distribution)

Lasso - ai ~ λ/2 exp (-λ|ai|)

Is it possible to implement such priors for "a"?
If not, is there another strategy I could implement in order to force an approximation for these priors?
(using Gaussian-like priors)

I was thinking, if maybe we could approximate the t distribution by the normal distribution as in...

http://www.m-hikari.com/ams/ams-2015/ams-49-52-2015/zogheibAMS49-52-2015.pdf

Would it be feasible?

Another strategy would be applying weights for the marker effects (using Ridge Regression), that would get updated after each iteration.

I really think INLA method is an opportunity for turning Bayesian approach more widely applied in genomics.

I don't really need to do Bayes A, B... etc.... exactly as they are.
If there is a way to adapt INLA in order to implement different priors for "a", or adapt a mixture in order to approximate it to less skewed normal, then I want to try it.

Again, sorry for the long massage Prof. Rue.
I've been thinking of it and got to write ideas down.

Best regards and thank you for the attention.

I am fitting a 'besag' model to the response variable 'number of calves of humpback whales' using a binomial distribution.

I have already tried a Poisson error distribution to the response 'number of calves of humpback whales' and the PIT showed the same pattern.

My dataset have a length of 123, where 56 observations are 0, 10 observations are 1,1 observation is 3 and 1 observation is 4. The rest is completed with NA (where I intend to predict occurrence).

The PIT histograms are available here: https://www.dropbox.com/sh/bydyihyl2lzl1a4/AAA9lX_yRLk7N3bf8koOKexma?dl=0

My questions are:
Can I present the results even with these PIT histograms?
Should I change anything in the model to improve PIT?

Thank you in advance for your help.

Best regards,
Heloise

I have another question related to the indexation and stack functionality when predicting.

I have 25 years of spatial data and I would like to predict the distribution of the process for each year. Is there any more elegant way of doing so than repeating the indexation and stacking the data for every year independently and then bind it all together?

e.g. using semi-code

for i in 1:25
A.i <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh,
                               group=i,
                               n.group=25)

                      A=list(A.i, 1),

                     tag='pred.i')

all.year.pred=inla.stack(pred.1, ...., pred.25)

Thank you very much,
Iosu

Donal

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA for genomic analysis.
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This thread has got me thinking too.

Another interesting idea is that both the t-distribution and the Laplace distribution can be formulated as a scale mixture of normals.  See link
below.  Basically, the t-distribution can be formulated by having a normally distributed random variable, whose variance is a gamma distribution, and
the Laplace is a normal whose variance is an exponential.

I'm not sure how this could relate to INLA though...  Sure, some of the randomness is normal but some of it is still non-normal.  Unless the gamma can
be approximated by some sort of truncated normal (and that a truncated normal is easier to deal with).

Also, for what it is worth (maybe not very much):  I have seen adaptive LASSO type work in genetics (QTL mapping, although I can't remember the
reference).  Here the penalty is weighted by the inverse of the *unpenalised* effects -- basically penalising small effects more than large effects.
This approach still has a number of desirable properties (although I can't remember exactly what. This approach may help maintain normal random
effects (just with different scales), just what the INLA machine is designed for.

Cheers,

Scott

messages.body_plain:
I've mused about similar issues (using continuous mixtures of
normals): one obvious problem is that you need a random effect for
every coefficient, so for most applications where you're interested in
doing this you would have to have far too many random effects to be
practical. There may also be problems with fitting, because the prior
has infinite density at zero (I dimly recall Håvard explaining this to
me a few years ago).

I can't see any good way around this: you could combine INLA with MCMC
(use MCMC for indicators of whether a variable is in the model). This
might not be very quick, although at least you would only have to
visit each combination of indicators once. I don't know if this would
really be better, though.

Bob

messages.subject_clean: Is it possible to use Weibull likelihood in a Two-Part model in R-INLA?
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I work with a Two-Part model with Generalized Gamma distributed non-zero observations and correlated random effects (like one described here <http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2824028/#FD13>), and analysis shows that the empirical distrbition of non-zero values of my DV can be pretty well approximated by Weibull distribution. I use SAS PROC NLMIXED for estimation, but, given small sample size (both small number of clusters and small cluster size) I also would like to check my inferences using Bayesian approach. I've got how to estimate two-part models that use, for example, gamma, normal, lognormal or skew normal likelihoods for continuous part in R-INLA (one may found basic ideas for INLA implementation here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/VN_qo24Xzx8>; correlated random effects are specified using iid2d model).

But I've also realized that, to use Weibull likelihood, I should specify my model as survival model. However, my data are not indeed "survival". messages.body_plain:
Yes, increasing or reducing the smoothness of a spline in INLA by reducing or increasing the number of knots is possible when using 2nd order B-spline basis functions with a 1d spde formulation. (With the rw2 implementation this can also be done in principle, but is messier)
The example in our recent J. Stat. Soft. is a starting point for coding that; just change the number of knots in that code.

Personally I think it's the wrong thing to do in principle, since it doesn't keep a clean separation between the continuous domain problem statement and the discretisation method; if the solution changes significantly from small changes in the discretisation, one should add nodes to reduce the approximation error, and not mix it into the model continuous model itself. Plenty of people working on splines however do this anyway, so I'm outnumbered on this issue at the moment.

If instead the model choice itself is done in the continuous formulation alone; i.e. by choosing the alpha parameter in the spde, one should simply have a large enough number of knots to give a good approximation of the spde. INLA supports values for alpha in between 1 and 2, so if rw1 is to rough and rw2 is too smooth, try the spde approximation for alpha=1.5 instead.

Finn

> to distribution from MCMC) and interpolating doesn't really help. Can
> I ask inla for more points or spread them out differently?

to follow up on this. the most recent testing version using more points
(unless the model is HUGE). if you're looking at hyperparameters, and
want to transform them, then its usually much safer, to start from the
marginals in `the internal scale', which is log(precision), say, and
transform from those.

like here

> r = inla(y ~ 1, data = data.frame(y = rnorm(10)))
> m1 = inla.tmarginal(function(prec) 1/sqrt(prec),
r$marginals.hyperpar[[1]])
> m2 = inla.tmarginal(function(logprec) 1/sqrt(exp(logprec)),
r$internal.marginals.hyperpar[[1]])

'm2' would be the most accurate one, in general.
